sections.title: One sentence
sections.body: Rules defining what kinds of things and relationships the model allows.

sections.title: In plain language
sections.body: Data is what you write down. A graph connects it. An ontology defines what those connections mean and which combinations are allowed.

sections.title: Concrete example
sections.body: In this repository, Technology USES Technology is allowed, while Document USES Person is not. Joule Studio and SAP BTP are illustrative names, not claims verified by this site.

sections.title: In this Knowledge OS
sections.body: Ontology.load reads config/ontology.yaml. Ontology.validate checks subject type, and for entity objects checks object type, predicate and allowed endpoints.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A graph can store a connection even when it makes no sense. Rules help reject invalid combinations before promotion.

sections.title: Technical detail
sections.body: The current validator returns early for scalar values. F5 records the unresolved predicate-validation gap. RUNS_ON and Platform are not registered in ontology 1.0.0.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.body: Open the checked implementation, tests, contracts and migrations below. These links identify evidence, not new verification.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Record the name Joule Studio. A name alone does not describe a connection or an allowed rule.

steps.title: Graph
steps.body: Connect two things: Technology → USES → Technology. This illustrates structure, not a verified product fact.

steps.title: Ontology
steps.body: Define allowed connections: Technology USES Technology is allowed; Document USES Person is rejected.
